extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of The Spectator / general literate public (early 18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short, moralizing, entertaining periodical essays in early-18th-century English (Spectator style) that combine wit, brevity, and moral instruction. Also commentary on English prose style and spoken language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Brevity / Sparing of Words
rubrics_metrics.description: The English language is wonderfully adapted to a man 'who is sparing of his Words, and an Enemy to Loquacity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise expression: 'when we are obliged to utter our Thoughts, we do it in the shortest way we are able, and give as quick a Birth to our Conception as possible.' This brevity reflects national temperament and suits periodical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Monosyllables for Readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The English abounds in monosyllables, 'which gives us an Opportunity of delivering our Thoughts in few Sounds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monosyllables may reduce elegance but increase readiness and clarity: prefer short, direct words to express ideas with dispatch in essays and conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraction / Elision of Syllables in Polysyllables
rubrics_metrics.description: In long words derived from Latin we 'contract the length of the Syllables ... to make them more proper for Dispatch, and more conformable to the Genius of our Tongue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural rapid pronunciation tends to shorten multi-syllable words (e.g., 'Liberty, Conspiracy, Theatre, Orator'); this can aid pace but be mindful of loss of solemnity or clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Excessive Clipping of Past-tense Endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Closing in one syllable the termination of our præterperfect tense, as in 'drown'd, walk'd, arriv'd' for 'drowned, walked, arrived', 'has very much disfigured the Tongue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with clipped -ed endings; while they quicken speech, they may 'disfigure' formal prose and reduce euphony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes from -eth to -s (preserve solemn forms in writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The abbreviation of several words terminated in 'eth' by substituting an 's' (drowns, walks, arrives) 'has wonderfully multiplied a Letter which was before too frequent in the English Tongue' and may displease foreigners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although such changes humour taciturnity, retain old terminations in writing and in solemn/religious contexts where appropriate to preserve formality and historical etymology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Pruning Spelling to Fit Pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Trimming words of 'superfluous Letters' to match pronunciation (as some authors attempted) 'would have confounded all our Etymologies, and have quite destroyed our Tongue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adjust orthography rashly to colloquial speech; preserve etymological spellings to maintain historical sense and the integrity of the language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Omit Necessary Particles (Maintain Grammatical Clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppressing several particles which must be produced in other tongues to make a sentence intelligible 'often perplexes the best Writers' — relatives (whom, which, or they) are at their mercy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance idiom and grammar: omission of particles for brevity may lead to ambiguity; an authoritative body ('an Academy') would settle disputes between grammar and idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of Subjects and Dense Paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for periodical writing: 'The Variety of your Subjects surprizes me ... each Paragraph is freight either with useful or delightful Notions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a wide variety of topics and ensure paragraphs carry substantive, useful or delightful ideas — compact, idea-rich paragraphs increase reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend Entertainment with Moral Improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Good periodical writing should 'charm the Fancy, sooth the Passions, and insensibly lead the Reader to that Sweetness of Temper ... rouse Generosity ... inculcate Humanity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine wit and amusement with moral instruction: the piece should both divert and improve the reader, affecting 'secret Springs of the Mind' without heavy-handed sermonizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility / Affordable Moral Instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator offers an 'infallible Cure of Vice and Folly, for the Price of One Penny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the periodical affordable and accessible; moral and intellectual benefits should be obtainable by a broad readership at low cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masterly Æquanimity as a Social Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Æquanimity in a Man's own Words and Actions 'will easily diffuse itself through his whole Family.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In social commentary (and in character sketches), endorse calmness and even temper in authority figures; such qualities produce harmonious households and form useful moral examples in essays.
